The future is bright and tricolor™ About us Privacy Policy Terms of Service Kostanyan, Brodsky explore expanded Armenian-Czech ties On September 4, as part of the Armenian president’s official visit to the Czech Republic, Deputy Foreign Minister Vahan Kostanyan met with Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Jiří Brodský and discussed opportunities to expand bilateral cooperation. The sides also addressed the Armenia-EU strategic partnership agenda and developments in the South Caucasus. Against the backdrop of the dynamic development of friendly relations between the two countries, the importance of reciprocal visits at the highest level was emphasized. The interlocutors identified high technology, artificial intelligence, water resources management, bilateral trade and tourism as promising areas of cooperation, agreeing to continue dialogue in these areas within the framework of intergovernmental commissions. The sides exchanged views on advancing the Armenia-EU strategic partnership agenda, developments in the South Caucasus, as well as a number of international agenda issues of mutual interest.

He was 94 years old. Raymond was born on July 20, 1932, in Lussinpiccolo, now Mali Lošinj, Croatia, to Erminia Ivancich. In 1944, during World War II, Raymond and his family were taken captive by invading forces. Nuns at a local church rescued Raymond and his brother, Claudio, helping the boys escape. Left orphaned by the war, the brothers owed their survival in part to the compassion of those who came to their aid. At 16, Raymond joined the merchant marine, working aboard ships that took him around the world. In 1951, he and his brother, Claudio Pragliola, arrived in the United States through Ellis Island. Raymond's original surname, Pragliola, was shortened to Prag as he began his new life in America. Settling in New York, Raymond worked as a bridge painter and carpenter to support himself and his brother. These demanding early years helped shape his lifelong determination and independence. Raymond later enlisted in the United States Marine Corps, serving in its aviation wing in Japan and Korea before transitioning to the United States Air Force. While stationed in Tripoli, Libya, he met Iolanda, the love of his life. They married in 1957, beginning a remarkable partnership and building a family together. During his 20-year military career, Raymond rose to the rank of Senior Master Sergeant, the Air Force's second-highest enlisted rank. His leadership responsibilities included work on programs involving the SR-71 Blackbird, B-52 bomber, and C-5 Galaxy. He earned numerous accolades before retiring in 1973, proud to have served his adopted country. His career reflected the discipline, high standards, and sense of responsibility that defined him. Following his military retirement, Raymond built a successful international business career. He founded a U.S.-based company representing multinational corporations, including Pratt & Whitney, Sikorsky, ABB, and Mitsubishi Power, in the aerospace and energy industries throughout Central and Eastern Europe. His work strengthened his ties to the region of his birth while allowing him to develop relationships across the world. Raymond believed deeply in giving back. A member of Rotary clubs in Southampton, New York, and Trieste, Italy, he also helped establish a Rotary club in his hometown of Mali Lošinj. Most meaningfully, he established a foundation supporting orphaned and disadvantaged children on the island. Having received the compassion of others as a child, he was determined to extend that same opportunity to future generations. His return to the island was both a homecoming and a chance to help others. An avid sailor, Raymond felt most at home on the water. He kept his sailboat in Trieste at Yacht Club Adriaco, where he had been a member since 1973. Fearless and strong-willed, he sailed year-round, even in winter. Family and friends remembered him heading out on windy days while other boats were returning to harbor. For Raymond, a strong wind was an invitation rather than a warning. He loved the challenge, the freedom, and sharing the sea with those close to him. Raymond and Iolanda spent 69 years together, sharing a love of travel and dividing their time among homes in New York, Italy, and Croatia. In each place, he maintained lasting friendships, remained connected to his roots, and made time for the people and communities important to him. Serious in manner and firm in his convictions, Raymond approached life with determination and purpose. His generosity was expressed not in grand words but in what he built, the people he supported, and the family he loved. He took immense pride in his sons and grandchildren. Raymond is survived by his beloved wife, Iolanda Prag; his sons, Henry and Anthony, and their wives, Ann and Cynthia, respectively; his grandchildren, Christian, Alexander, Massimo, and Giancarlo; and his brother, Claudio. He will be remembered for his strength, perseverance, generosity, and devotion to family. From a childhood marked by war and loss to a life of service, adventure, and giving back, Raymond leaves a legacy that will endure for generations.
